Is it hard to separate your friendships from the need to criticise during the creative process?

"...in a day?" Haha, I wish the development was going that rapidly. If we all lived in one incubator, and only ate and developed, ate and developed... Well, I don't think I'd be your best bet for this kind of AMA since I'm slowly planning my exit on programming and computer sciences in general. Nothing wrong with it, I simply found out it may not exactly be the career for me.

But I'm glad if I can give you some advice about what you asked.

  • How's life for me? Not great, I had many things happen to me in the last 5 years (mostly personal, but some professional too) that put me in a though spot. I'm working for the public sector almost out of necessity. I earn enough to provide for my family, but it's at the price of my sanity.

  • What were my studies like? I studied and live outside of the USA, so maybe my experience would be different than what most people would have lived on an English speaking website. I'd say I mostly enjoyed my studies actually. I enjoyed especially the courses related to management and artificial intelligence. I found one project we did for artificial intelligence I, about programming a bot with basic linguistic semantics "understanding" absolutely fascinating. I speak a few languages, so linguistics has always been an interest of mine (I actually did an AMA about that if you're interested). The subject (of computer science) is of great interest to me, it's only the type of job we get in that doesn't appeal to me anymore.

  • Emacs vs Vi? Honestly, it all boils down to personal preference, there's no objectively better option, only preferred taste in one.

  • Windows or Linux (or Mac)? Similar to the previous question. I've worked only on Windows, but I would really like to know Linux better (I actually plan on creating a business on this in the next few years). I think Mac has tremendous advantages for certain persons/tasks. Once you stop with the fanboy crap arguments and start to evaluate things (OSes, programs, programming languages, etc.) objectively based on real pros and cons, you realize most have good points and most have bad points. Windows is the most used, it makes it the most well known system and the easier to develop for and distribute. Linux is based on solid principles and (mostly) open source, It can be tweaked like no other OS, but it's not for most casual users (we're getting there slowly). Mac (It's the one I know the least) is a design ideal, it appeals to people who want something that works well and is nice to look at, without changing it to fit one's way to work. If you don't want to understand how something works, just something that works fine and look nice, Mac is for you.

  • Tips for an aspiring (since two years) programmer? Find projects that you like working on and keep that separate from the ones that make you money. The most profitable projects are generally the most boring. That's fine, but be aware of it. As long as you can work on something that makes you happy, even if it's on the side and doesn't pay a dime, you should be fine. And if you're one of the few that gets to work on a fun project that also pays well, then good for you!

Some more technical details for anyone interested:

  • Cross-platform. The game works on both linux and windows, and would be on mac too, if I just had someone to build it (I don't own a mac).
  • C++, Lua as languages.
  • Built from the core - no UnrelEngine or Unity, or anything like that. The game was meant as a learning experience (tho it became much more), so I have only used lower-level libraries like SDL, Box2D, OpenGL, freetype...
  • Scriptable mobs, levels. Their behavior is stated in lua files, so no need for me to modify the source and rebuild.
  • Not done. I keep thinking "it will just be a few months more".
  • IDE: code::blocks. I wish they'd release an update.
  • Source versioning: Git.
  • Source hosting: Bitbucket.
  • Building: I don't know "make" yet... ;(
  • Level design: After writing my own editor in-game I realised that it was complete trash, so we moved to blender. Turned out even tho writing plugins isn't easy, the returns are thousand-fold.
  • Programmer setup: I have two monitors! Yay! Also, I recommend "Microsoft Natural Ergonomic 4000" as a keyboard. I work both on windows and linux, tho I just lost my linux computer so we'll see when I get a new one.
Wait, lucid dreams? Sounds super cool, need more info!

Well, lucid dreams fit really well into our game because of multiple things. For one, we have a girl on the team that has this sort of fascination with lucid dreams, so from the beginning, she wanted to explore that concept in the game somehow. Second, in a lucid dream you can manipulate the world with your thoughts, and that fits well with our mechanic of being able to move anything in the level with the cursor, and the physics simulation. So when the player lifts something up with the mouse, it's like the main character were doing it with his mind! He can even lift himself up!

Also, we are adding some restraints to this, which will change during the course of the game. Examples would be not being able to "hold" something for longer than some period of time, or not in certain areas...

I guess, since he meets his sister (oh and also other classmates, becasue they're getting the sleep sickness too) in his dreams, the game explores the concept of shared dreams too.
I have a fascination with lucid dreams as well so you'll have to keep me posted on this game somehow :)
How did you get your start in game design/dev? What would you tell an aspiring game developer?

Do note that I'm not doing this professionally, I was just accepted to high school (Yay!) so now I will finally be able to study programming officially, but the game gets made in the spare time between school and, well, life.

That being said, I was awfully arrogant just having learned a little bit of C++ and deciding "Oh well, I'm going to make a game! Maybe we'll even sell it on steam!", but on the other hand, I would not have done anything differently if I could go back. This game has forced me to deeply learn C++, Lua, and a whole lot of "good programming" practices, as well as learning the technology behind games, how they work, different ways of doing this and that, algorithms, rendering, everything!

I even got some lessons I never expected to get, and I'm talking about team management and cooperation around a product. For a time we had another programmer on the team (I wish I had one now), super-intelligent guy, talented as hell. Anyways, he was a great person to discuss programming with (how are we going to do this and that? What do you think?), but he never really added anything to the game code itself. He was constantly saying he had other stuff going on (and he sure did, not saying he was lying, but hey, I had stuff too, and somehow I was making the time, so I was a bit frustrated). I was letting it slide, but when summer was approaching* I was expecting him to get time for doing some actual work. I was bugging him more and more about basically "hey could you tell me when you'll get to work?" (I used other words, ofc.). And after some evading, he basically told me he wasn't planning on working on the game at all, he had other projects, etc. I felt cheated and abandoned (the coding was a heavy workload, i'm telling you), but I can't say it was his fault, might just as well have been me having too high hopes and stuff, assuming too many things... He was of course free to leave the project at any time, it's not like I was paying him, I had just assumed that he was sharing my desire to make a game, but apparently that wasn't the case.

If anyone wants to get into game programming, well first off, go listen to someone who is actually in the industry and not me. But beside that, I'd tell them that programming isn't for everyone, and it's harder than you think, but if you still have a desire to be on the credits after the future "Half-Life 2" (this is my dream), the courage or foolishness to say "hey, I'm going to make a game!" can get you a long way. I would never had learned so much about programming in this short time if it wasn't for the game I was making, and I would not have kept making it if it wasn't for the sense of responsibility to my team, which had dedicated their time to it too.

(This has become too long to proofread, please excuse any typos, hope it answers your question).

* Oh wait, that must mean I've been on this game for 1 and a half years!
What are your plans for publishing? Do you have any? Will you try to sell it or distribute it for free?

We have no actual plans, but the general idea was to sell it on steam. Then again, the general idea was also "We'll have it done in two months tops".

For me, I'll be happy if I get it to a level where other people would enjoy playing it. The question also remains what will happen with the group, now that we've all gone off to college and don't go to the same school anymore. I have some who will probably want to keep making it, but not sure about all of them.

Ultimately, if the group should disband, I'd probably not bother with steam and just open-source and display it on my resume.
